subject: arcadeCabinet
pitch:
Category: Object.
Subject: 1980s arcade cabinet.
Style: synthwave.
reasoning:
This is a static object, so I can skip joints and rigging entirely and just build the geometry under a plain root group. I'm planning the arcade cabinet carefully using the safe builder API—parts, extrusions, lathes, and decals—to construct the synthwave-style 1980s cabinet since I won't be able to test it directly.

I'm sketching out real-world dimensions (roughly 1.8m tall, 0.68m wide, 0.9m deep) and working out the classic upright cabinet silhouette in side profile: kickplate base, angled control panel jutting forward, a recessed sloped monitor bezel, and a protruding marquee up top, all mapped out in z/y coordinates with the front facing +Z. I'm also noting that the glow kit import will throw errors on painted parts, so I'll need to stick with flat colors or textures for any glowing elements.

Still writing coordinate outline...

Still plotting cabinet coordinates...

For the side panels I'm thinking synthwave art—dark navy base with diagonal neon pink/cyan stripes and a grid, maybe sun and palm silhouettes. Since extrude doesn't support textures, I could project a decal onto the flat side face instead, treating it like an SVG projected onto the surface.

Actually safer approach: keep most of the model as solid-color paint, then add separate textured planes just off each side face for the art. I'm now working out orientation—placing a plane at each side with the right facing direction, and figuring out which way "up" and "right" map for a viewer standing to the side looking inward, so the artwork reads correctly rather than mirrored.

Since the side art will mirror between the +X and -X panels, I'll just treat it as abstract, text-free texture so the mirroring doesn't matter. I need to clip the side SVG art to the cabinet's silhouette rather than a plain rectangle, so I'm computing the outline in SVG coordinates using the same plane dimensions (width 0.92, height spanning y 0 to 1.82) to build the clip path.

Now I'm setting up a vertical gradient for the side art, running from deep indigo through purple toward magenta.

I'll set glow strength to 0.7 for the side art so emissive scales down a bit rather than full intensity. For the cabinet, I'm planning T-molding as thin glowing tubes swept along the silhouette's outline, using a closed polyline with rounded corners so the trim wraps smoothly around the edges without needing joint skinning since it's static.

To keep corner handling safe at the sharp 90° bends, I'm considering building the trim from individual rod segments with small spheres at the vertices instead of relying on a single swept closed polyline, since that avoids any ambiguity about how corners get rounded.

For the back panel, I'm placing a thin dark plate between the sides with a recessed door look and a few vent slits for detail. Then I'm starting the front lower body with a coin door panel box positioned near the front edge of the sides.

Now I'm adding the front panel between the sides in dark plum, plus a coin door section with metallic plate, coin slots, neon-lit return buttons, and a coin-return flap, followed by a recessed kick panel at the base.

Adding a glowing cyan underglow strip at the kick panel, plus a textured neon front panel with synthwave grid art and "INSERT COIN" text. Now I'm shifting to the control panel: defining its slanted surface geometry from the front lip to the back edge as a thin rotated box.

I'm thinking the deck fills the space between the front panel and sides, topped with a textured overlay plane for the control panel art—joystick holes, buttons, player-start layout. I'm calculating the plane's size and center position along the slanted surface, plus the normal direction needed to offset it slightly off the geometry so it doesn't z-fight.

Working out plane orientation...

For the joystick layout, I'm planning two sticks for a classic 2-player arrangement (P1 on the left, P2 on the right), each with two colored buttons (pink and cyan) plus lit center start buttons. I'm constructing each joystick from a base disc, chrome shaft, and a saturated colored ball top, with the buttons built as lathed cylinders with chamfered edges and a glow effect.

Now I'm working out the geometry for positioning parts on the sloped control panel, defining a helper function that maps across-panel and along-slope coordinates plus height into actual 3D points, so I can place the sticks and buttons correctly relative to the panel's front lip and back edge, accounting for which side is the viewer's left versus +X in the model.

Laying out the control panel elements: joysticks near the outer edges (x≈±0.2-0.22) with button clusters inward from them, plus small centered start buttons, staggered slightly in depth for a natural arcade cabinet feel.

Now I'm thinking through the monitor bezel — figuring out its sloped housing shape as a trapezoidal cross-section extruded along the width, which forms the recessed frame holding the screen behind the marquee and above the deck.

I'm calculating the slope geometry for the bezel surface, figuring out where the screen plane sits versus the bezel art frame with its neon-pink border, placing the screen slightly behind the bezel's transparent window so both layer correctly.

I'll draw the bezel as a full rectangle with a cut-out hole using an SVG mask, placing the screen plane slightly behind it so the hole reveals the screen rather than the wedge surface, keeping the planes a couple millimeters apart to avoid z-fighting. Now I'm working out the orientation vectors for positioning this plane correctly on the sloped surface.

For the marquee I'm designing a lightbox-style sign with a chrome/black bezel and neon cyan outline tubes, spanning between the side panels. I'll name the game "NEON DRIVE '84" and texture the front plane with a purple sunset gradient and chrome-gradient italic retro lettering outlined in pink.

Since font availability in the rasterizer is uncertain, I'll use bold sans-serif with a skew transform to fake italics, with glow set to 1.2. Above the marquee I'm adding a dark purple top cap that slightly overhangs the sides, sitting right at the top of the cabinet with a neon edge, keeping the total cabinet height around 1.84 and making sure the floor and side panels align properly at y=0. I'm also considering adding a neon topper sign above the cabinet, like a triangle or ring, to complete the synthwave arcade look.

I'll place slotted speaker grilles on the lower front panel, then build out the coin door geometry — metal plate, glowing coin slots, push-button returns, and a recessed coin cup — positioned above a lower textured panel that could carry a neon sun logo.

Writing SVG code...

Still working out panel placement...

Adding lit rings above slots, return buttons, a coin cup with flap, and corner screws. I'm also sketching back-panel details like vents and a power cord sweeping from the inlet down to the floor for a subtle finishing touch.

I'll skip levelers and leg bolts since the cabinet sits flush on the ground, and move on to building the joystick: a dark base plate, a dust-washer cone, a chrome shaft, and a ball top.

For the ball top and buttons, I'm settling on a synthwave palette — hot pink, cyan, purple, orange, yellow, dark indigo — with a concave dish profile for the buttons and pink/cyan combos assigned to each player.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the deck surface: computing a slope vector between the front and back lip points, deriving a normal vector, and defining a helper function that maps x, v (slope position), and h (height offset) into a 3D point on the deck.

For the deck artwork, I'm mapping a 2D SVG coordinate system onto this plane, flipping the vertical axis so the back of the deck corresponds to the top of the drawing, and sketching a dark gradient background with neon outlines around the stick and button positions.

Now I'm working out the cabinet's lip geometry, adding cyan and magenta glowing trim lines along the front edge, then starting on the monitor wedge's extrusion profile.

I'm refining the deck polygon coordinates, adjusting the chamfer edge to match the side outline at z=.40 instead of .38, and checking that the front panel box (y up to .78, z .37-.40) doesn't collide with the deck's angled underside.

I also need to check the gap between the wedge top (y=1.56) and the marquee bottom (y=1.58) at z=.30, since there's a small discontinuity there. I'll adjust the marquee box to start at y=1.57 instead, adding a small ledge from the side outline to close the gap cleanly.

Still placing geometry...

That gives 28 capsules total, which seems fine. I'm checking the capsule helper's signature to confirm radius and color ordering, and whether it returns a Sweep-compatible shape so glow can wrap it with the `sides` option set to 6.

Now I'm working out the side silhouette coordinates in SVG space, converting the outline's z/y points into pixel positions by mapping z through a 100x scale offset from 0.50 and y through a similar offset from 1.82, then listing out the vertex pairs that define the side profile shape.

I'm designing the side artwork as a synthwave scene: a night sky fading into a gradient sunset with a striped sun near the horizon, mountain silhouettes, and a neon perspective grid for the lower portion, with an inset neon outline tracing the shoe's silhouette edge.

For the sun, I'll use a gradient from yellow to pink with a mask of horizontal bands that thicken toward the bottom to create that retro cut-sun effect. Then I'm setting up the marquee SVG viewbox with a gradient background, partial sun, grid lines, stars, and a bold italic "NEON DRIVE" title text.

Writing SVG text styling...

Now I'm building the screen SVG with a sky gradient, striped sun, mountains, perspective road, a car sprite with taillights, speed lines, and HUD text elements.

Adding scanline and vignette overlays to the screen, then moving to the bezel SVG where I'm cutting a rounded hole for the screen to fit centered within the sloped bezel plane.

Drawing SVG hole path...

Also reconsidering sizing: I want the screen plane slightly larger than the bezel hole so its edges stay hidden behind the bezel, so I'll make the screen 48x39 while the hole stays 46x37.

For the control deck I'm sizing the SVG viewbox at 590x247 scaled to 1024px. I'm deciding to skip extra flourishes like glass curvature, back vents detail, and floor glow to keep things focused.

I'm settling on a neon tube frame lining the marquee front and sides in cyan/pink, plus a decal sticker on the lower front panel, player labels and stick shafts on the control panel, and a coin door — while skipping rubber feet since the cabinet sides already meet the floor.

Now I'm adding a kickplate with a pink underglow strip, and thinking through the overall part budget — aiming for efficient helper functions given the time constraints rather than hitting the full 180-340 part target. I'm planning real geometry for speaker grilles (two grilles of 8 slots each on the lower front) instead of relying on texture, and confirming the side texture plane sits slightly offset so the extruded edges still show painted trim. For materials, I'm consolidating painted parts under one shared material while keeping separate materials per texture plane, and tallying up how many distinct textures I'll need across the side, front, and deck surfaces.

I'm expanding that texture list to include the screen bezel, marquee, back panel (with a warning sticker and vents), and a coin door label reading "INSERT COIN 25¢" — bringing the total to around nine textures, which should keep the flat color count under the 64 limit. For paints, I'm sketching out a side panel paint using noise and gradient mixing functions from the SDK, and considering a metal paint from the clockwork kit for the coin plate, while double-checking that import path actually exists in the library.

Now I'm building out a color palette for the whole cabinet — night purple, plum, violet, pink, cyan, sunset orange, yellow, black, and chrome tones — and sketching a gradient paint for the side panels that transitions from a deep violet at the bottom to a darker plum near the top, keeping in mind that most of it will be hidden behind the art plane except along the visible edges.

Setting up the imports and metadata for the build...

Adding box and cylinder helper functions...

I'm checking texture handling for colored SVGs, glow effects, and material setup, making sure textured parts get one material per texture with transparent cutouts. Now I'm working through the deck geometry extrusion logic, figuring out how outline coordinates relate to the origin point.

For the side panels, I'm defining typed outline arrays and confirming they're compatible with the OutlinePoint type, keeping corners sharp by default and considering a small bevel for nicer edges.

For the neon trim, I'm positioning the capsule centered right on the silhouette boundary so it wraps the edge like a T-molding rim, protruding slightly beyond the art plane rather than sitting purely inside or outside it.

Now I'm assigning colors to each edge segment going around the perimeter, alternating mostly pink with cyan accents at the bottom and transition points to distinguish the deck-lip from the monitor surface.

I'm writing a helper function that converts the normalized side-profile points into SVG path coordinates, scaling and flipping them to build the silhouette path string.

With that set up, I'm now drafting the full SVG markup: a clip path from the silhouette, a scattering of small pale stars randomly placed in the upper region, and gradient definitions for the sky (deep purple to magenta) and sun.

Still writing SVG layers...

Adding more stripe polygons...

I'll skip extra bottom text to avoid clutter and instead place blinking "INSERT COIN" text above the door around y 15-18, keeping it clear of the pinstripes and door start at y 19.

Now I'm working out the arcade deck art, computing the SVG coordinates for the joystick and button positions for both players by converting their normalized x/v values into pixel space, placing concentric pink rings around each stick and mirroring the layout symmetrically for player two.

Writing screen gradients and scanlines...

Adding HUD text, scanlines, vignette, and glare overlay effects, then computing the road perspective math for vanishing point, dashed center line, and ground grid lines...

Still writing SVG code for the marquee logo...

Now I'm planning the bezel SVG and a small back-label sticker with warning chevrons and "NEON DRIVE · SERIAL 0084" text.

I'll skip the coin door texture since the front art already covers "INSERT COIN," landing on seven textures total plus paints. Now I'm setting up the cabinet geometry, defining width and thickness constants and extruding the side panels symmetrically from the centerline.

I'm working out the placement of the art planes on each side panel, checking how the bevel affects the flat surface area and making sure the local coordinate orientation matches correctly between the left and right sides so the artwork maps properly in each direction.

For the -X side, I realize the local right-vector flips to +Z, which would mirror the texture relative to the baked silhouette, causing a mismatch with the cabinet outline. To fix this, I'll generate a separate texture for each side (eight total) rather than reusing one, wrapping the art content in a mirrored transform group when needed so the silhouette lines up correctly on both sides.

Now I'm sizing the front panel body and its face art placement, placing the box and determining the plane dimensions and centers based on the panel's y-range.

Still positioning kick plate and glow strips...

Now I'm designing the coin door: a painted steel plate centered around z=0.4075, with the underlying art plane sitting just behind it. I'm working out the door's inset frame and the two coin mechanism bezels on either side.

Adding more door details...

Adding joystick geometry...

I'm also adding start buttons with glow in yellow and orange, confirming the lathe function works fine with Vector3 directions for axis and position. For the monitor, I'm extruding a wedge shape with a dark color, checking that the outline doesn't self-intersect and that the hollow interior stays hidden since it's enclosed by the sides and topped by the wedge.

Now I'm working out the screen placement on the sloped surface — computing the slope vector between the bottom and top points, finding its length and midpoint, then deriving the unit vector and outward normal to orient the screen plane correctly against the slope.

I'll skip the glass bulge and trim lip as unnecessary detail. For the marquee, I'm positioning an extruded outline shape as the dark art panel above the screen, sized to fit the front face, with neon capsule frames bordering it along the top and sides.

Now I'm adding the top cap as a thin box slightly overhanging the marquee front edge, with a dark purple color, plus a couple of cyan capsule trim pieces along its front and back edges for a neon accent.

For the back of the cabinet, I'm adding a dark panel matching the side edges, a back access door with vent slots arranged in a row, and a small back-facing label plane—working out its local orientation so the drawing axes align correctly when facing the -Z direction.

I'm also placing the power inlet socket on the back, a small switch, and routing the power cord with a smooth curved path down to the floor, keeping the geometry above ground level.

I'm deciding against extra decorative elements like neon halos, antennas, or seam lines to keep things simple, and moving on to writing the side paint shader with a smoothstep gradient function.

Writing shader code...

Writing the stars helper and side-art generator, adjusting star radius scaling so they're visible at raster size...

Still writing gradients and mask...

Still writing SVG defs...

Still writing SVG code...

Still laying out the start buttons and labels, swapping "1P"/"2P" for simpler "1"/"2" markers in yellow to avoid text collisions, then placing the "NEON DRIVE" title in pink italic near the top and checking it doesn't overlap the B2 buttons below it.

Now I'm drafting the arcade cabinet bezel artwork with an SVG gradient background and a rounded rectangular screen hole, adding a neon-style border outline around the opening to give it that glowing cabinet look.

Still writing SVG code...

I'm also planning the marquee artwork separately—a retro sunset sky with a chrome gradient title, horizon grid, and a glowing sun behind the text.

Now setting glow intensities across elements: brighter for the screen and marquee, more subdued for front and side art so things stay balanced visually. Starting to write out the full code for the arcade cabinet builder, defining constants for metal paints and SVG textures before the build function assembles everything.

Working out small helper utilities, like a position vector shortcut and a box-geometry wrapper, and figuring out the right color/type signature so they integrate cleanly with the builder's part function.

Adding a plane helper function too, and now I'm thinking through whether the default "up" vector will orient the deck plane correctly when its direction is nearly vertical with a slight tilt — need to check how the local Y axis projects relative to world up for that slope.

Now I'm defining a trim helper using capsules for side details...

Still writing build function...

I'm setting up the color palette (pink, cyan, yellow, orange, violet, night tones) and looping over the two player positions to place their deck sticks, balls, and buttons with mirrored colors for each side.

Now I'm checking the button placements and spacing against the stick base to make sure nothing overlaps on the deck, and verifying that my deckPoint function correctly scales along the slope vector for different v values.

I'm working out the coin door's coin plate, bezel, and ring glow geometry—setting z-depths for each layered piece (plate front, mech bezel, ring) and mapping left/right sides to pink/cyan colors.

Still placing the slot glow, dark slot, return button, and coin cup/flap, figuring out their positions, sizes, and colors so they sit correctly relative to the ring button above the slot.

Checking that the plate's y-range still fits all components after adjusting the bezel height so it doesn't overlap the return button, repositioning the slot and screws accordingly, then moving toward writing out the full code for the machine including the cord sweep detail.

Writing screen art code...

Adding roadside poles and the car...

Adding more wheels and a spoiler...

I'm also sanity-checking the overall SVG dimensions against the screen size, and roughly tallying up the part count across all the sections (sides, trims, coin door, deck, monitor, marquee, cap, back) to make sure the design stays reasonably detailed without overdoing it.
